questions.question: What does a 'graph representation' of a figure-counting problem use as its nodes and edges?
options: Colors as nodes, shapes as edges
The figure's vertices as nodes and its line segments as edges
Only the figure's area as a single node
Random labels unrelated to the figure
questions.rationale: A graph representation models the figure's vertices as nodes and its line segments as edges connecting them, the same idea used elsewhere in structured reasoning.

questions.question: What is the 'closed-path concept' central to in graph-based figure counting?
options: Drawing decorative borders
A valid geometric figure corresponds to a closed path (cycle) in the graph representation
Only open, non-closed paths count as figures
Counting the number of nodes only
questions.rationale: In this framework, a valid geometric figure corresponds to a closed path — a cycle — traced through the graph's nodes and edges.

questions.question: In graph terms, a triangle corresponds to what?
options: A 2-cycle
A 3-cycle (a closed path of 3 edges/vertices)
A 4-cycle
An open path with no cycle
questions.rationale: A triangle, having 3 vertices and 3 connecting edges forming a closed loop, corresponds to a 3-cycle in graph terms.

questions.question: In graph terms, a rectangle corresponds to what?
options: A 3-cycle
A 4-cycle (a closed path of 4 edges/vertices)
A 5-cycle
A single edge
questions.rationale: A rectangle, with its 4 vertices and 4 connecting edges forming a closed loop, corresponds to a 4-cycle.

questions.question: Why are 'graph cycles not always geometric figures'?
options: All graph cycles are always valid figures
A cycle might not correspond to a straight-edged, non-self-intersecting geometric shape, so each candidate cycle must still be validated geometrically
Cycles only exist in triangular grids
Because graphs cannot represent geometric shapes at all
questions.rationale: A cycle in the abstract graph doesn't automatically guarantee a valid geometric shape — it must still be checked against the actual geometric constraints of the figure.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'figure-counting checklist'?
options: To replace the need for any formulas
To systematically verify each step (basic figures, composite figures, double-counting checks) hasn't been skipped before finalizing a count
To list every possible color a figure could be
To only be used after the count is already finalized
questions.rationale: A checklist ensures every stage of the counting process — basic figures, composites, double-counting checks — has actually been carried out before the final answer is given.

questions.question: In a 2x3 grid of unit squares, how many 1x1 squares are there?
questions.rationale: A 2-row by 3-column grid contains 2 x 3 = 6 unit (1x1) squares.

questions.question: In that same 2x3 grid, how many 2x2 squares are there?
questions.rationale: A 2x2 square can start at either of 2 possible horizontal positions within a 3-wide, 2-tall grid, giving 2 total 2x2 squares.

questions.question: So what is the total number of squares of all sizes in a 2x3 grid?
questions.rationale: 6 unit squares plus 2 of size 2x2 gives a total of 8 squares.

questions.question: When 'counting rectangles excluding squares' in a grid, what must you do?
options: Only count 1x1 shapes
Count all rectangles of every size, then subtract out the ones that happen to be squares (equal width and height)
Count only rectangles with an odd perimeter
Ignore the grid's boundary lines entirely
questions.rationale: Since every square is technically a rectangle, excluding squares means counting all rectangles first and then subtracting the count of squares from that total.
